scenes.imageLabel: Clear sky · Punjab and Haryana · 3 Nov 2023
scenes.question: A field that burns once, or a factory that never sleeps?

beats.say: Think of a street at night. A birthday candle glows once and is gone. A street lamp glows every single night. If you counted every light you ever saw, the lamp would win by far, even though it is not a celebration.

Brick kilns, gas flares and steel plants are the street lamps of the fire record. A rice field burns once. Formula eight, persistence, measures how often a site is seen hot, so steady industrial heat does not fill up the farm-fire calendar.

parts.say: On the left is p x, the persistence of site x. It is a share between zero and one.

On top, we count the days the site was hot. Underneath, we count the days the site could have been seen: days when the satellite had a clear look, not cloud. Dividing by calendar days instead would make cloudy places look less persistent.

And if the site could never be seen at all, persistence is unknown. It is not zero. We simply had no chance to look. A cut-off for calling a site persistent, for example 0.20, is a hypothesis still to be fitted on labelled sites, not a fixed constant.

steps.label: Days seen hot
steps.say: Here is an illustrative kiln, a made-up example to explain the idea. It was seen hot on 300 days.

steps.label: Days it could be seen
steps.say: It could have been seen on 365 days.

steps.label: Persistence
steps.say: Divide, and the kiln's persistence is 0.82. A paddy field hot on 7 of 365 days scores only 0.02. In the real archive, sites that FIRMS marks as static sources were hot on a median of 49 days, while farm-fire sites were hot on a median of just 3.

beats.say: On the left is the share of sites hot on at least a given number of days, from 2012 to 2026, for farm-fire sites and for FIRMS static-source sites, on log scales. The static sites stay hot far longer.
On the right, the static-source detections in red stand out against all the vegetation-fire detections in grey. FIREWORK removed 17,588 static-source detections.

beats.label: Hot pixels by ground type
beats.say: On the FIREWORK website, open the Sources page. The side panel splits hot pixels by the type of ground they sit on. Persistence is one of the clues for calling a site agricultural, industrial or uncertain.

beats.label: Method
beats.say: The method section explains the rule. Be aware: the clear-day counts are not loaded yet for this region, so the exact persistence score is still pending. We only know the busiest static site has a persistence of at least 0.16.

points: Persistence = hot days ÷ days the site could be seen
Clouded days do not count as looks
No looks at all means unknown, not zero

beats.say: So, to remember: divide the days a site was hot by the days it could be seen. Fields score low, factories score high, and the farm-fire calendar stays about farms.
